A Love Letter to the AI Skeptics: Why There’s Reason for Optimism
Choosing optimism about AI is a necessary act of discipline in a culture that increasingly equates cynicism with intelligence.

![](/images/articles/a-love-letter-to-the-ai-skeptics-why-there-s-reason-for-optimism/1775246848111.png)\
have been called a glass-half-full person for most of my career, and I have never once taken that as an insult. In a world that increasingly mistakes cynicism for intelligence and anxiety for depth, I have come to believe that optimism is not naive at all. It is a discipline. It is a decision. It is, in many ways, an act of courage.

Right now, we are surrounded by people who seem almost emotionally committed to telling the darkest possible story about the future. Every conversation about technology somehow slides toward collapse. **Every conversation about AI seems to arrive at the same exhausted conclusion, that we should mostly be afraid, mostly pull back, and mostly brace ourselves for loss.** Of course, there are risks. Of course, there are serious questions. Of course, we need ethics, regulation, discernment, and accountability. But I cannot help feeling that something has gone wrong in the spirit of the conversation when awe has disappeared entirely and when gratitude has become almost unfashionable.

Because if we are honest, and if we are willing to step back from the panic of the daily news cycle, **this is an astonishing moment to be alive**. We are living in a time of extraordinary human capability, and I do not think we talk nearly enough about what a privilege that is. We speak so often about what might go wrong that we forget to notice what is already going right. **We forget that we are surrounded by tools, discoveries, and forms of connection that previous generations would have considered miraculous.** We forget that progress has always arrived carrying complexity, and that complexity is not the same thing as doom.

I feel this especially when I think about my own family. My father is sick with Parkinson's. My mother is living with Alzheimer's. There is nothing abstract about that kind of reality. It is intimate, exhausting, heartbreaking, and deeply humbling. It changes the way you listen to people. It changes the way you hear conversations about innovation, because suddenly you are no longer interested in clever posturing about whether technology feels unsettling. You care about whether something can actually help**. You care about whether a system can notice a change earlier than a human eye might, whether it can help manage medications and appointments, whether it can reduce confusion, whether it can give a caregiver a little relief, whether it can preserve a little more dignity, a little more continuity, a little more independence for people you love.**

When technology enters that kind of space, it stops being theoretical. It stops being a trend deck and starts becoming a form of mercy. That is why I find the flattening of AI into one big fear story so frustrating. Pe**ople talk as though the only morally serious posture is suspicion, but that is a luxury of distance.** When you have watched illness rearrange a family, you do not dismiss the possibility that better tools could ease suffering. You do not roll your eyes at the idea that intelligence, whether human or machine-augmented, might help us care for one another more effectively. You do not treat that as hype. You treat it as hope.

The same is true in healthcare more broadly. We are entering an era in which earlier detection, better pattern recognition, more personalized treatment, and smarter systems of prevention are no longer fantasies. They are becoming part of the architecture of reality. That should stop us in our tracks. **There are very few moments in history when a generation can say, with a straight face, that we may be participating in a meaningful reduction of human suffering at scale. We may be one of those generations.** That should not make us arrogant, but it should make us grateful.

And it is not only healthcare. It is the capability itself that is being reimagined. We are seeing systems that help people communicate differently, move differently, navigate differently, and participate more fully in the world after injury or limitation. We are seeing technology not simply as a convenience, but as a way of restoring agency. For all the noise and nonsense that surrounds this moment, that remains the thing I cannot get over: we are building tools that, at their best, expand what a human life can be.

I have also been thinking a lot about what this moment looks like beyond the narrow lens through which the West so often views innovation. A friend of mine was recently telling me about the impact AI is already having across parts of Africa, and what struck me was not some glossy narrative about disruption. It was the grounded, practical beauty of people using these tools to solve real problems, create new access, build businesses faster, and leap over barriers that used to feel permanent. She was talking about entrepreneurs, educators, builders, and communities not waiting for permission to participate in the future, but actively shaping it for themselves. **That matters to me because it is a reminder that the story of technological progress does not belong to one geography, one company, or one class of people.** There is extraordinary news coming from places the global narrative too often reduces to challenge alone, and I think we have a responsibility to tell those stories too. Hope should not be provincial. Possibility should not be gatekept.

And then, of course, I think about Ella.

When I look at my niece, I do not want to hand her a worldview built out of inherited panic. I do not want her to absorb the stale anxieties of adults who have decided that fear sounds more sophisticated than faith. I **do not want her to grow up believing that the future is something that happens to her while she stands in the doorway trying to protect herself from it. I want her to understand that she was born into a moment of immense possibility, and that her job is not to shrink in the face of that possibility, but to meet it with character, imagination, and courage.**

That may be the part I care about most. The next generation is listening to us, even when we think they are not. They are listening to the way we talk about work, about technology, about the planet, about institutions, about one another. They are absorbing the emotional posture we bring to change. And I worry that too many adults are passing down their burnout, their cynicism, and their ambient despair as though those things were wisdom. They are not wisdom. They are often just unprocessed fear with better vocabulary.

Of course, young people should understand the risks. T**hey should know that power must be watched, that systems must be designed responsibly, that bias can be encoded, that jobs will evolve, that ethics matter, and that not every new capability is automatically a social good.** But there is a profound difference between teaching responsibility and teaching dread. One invites a person into adulthood. The other makes them smaller before they have even begun.

I want Ella, and her generation, to inherit a truer story than that. I want them to know that they are stepping into a world with extraordinary tools in their hands, and that those tools can be used to make life more creative, more humane, more connected, and more meaningful. I want them to believe that progress is still possible, that invention is still noble, that building is still beautiful, and that the right response to a complicated future is not paralysis but participation.

This is where I think the pessimists get it wrong. **They imagine that optimism means ignoring what is difficult, when in fact real optimism is forged in contact with difficulty. It is not a refusal to see the darkness. It is a refusal to give the darkness the final word.** It is what allows us to look clearly at illness and still believe in better care, to look at broken systems and still believe in redesign, to look at inequality and still believe in wider access, to look at a generation coming up behind us and decide that what we owe them is not our fear, but our best thinking and our boldest hope.

**So yes, let us ask hard questions. Let us build responsibly. Let us challenge concentrated power, scrutinize incentives, and protect what is human and fragile and irreplaceable. But while we do that, let us also remember to look up. Let us remember that this is not the end of human relevance. It may be the beginning of one of the most meaningful expansions of human capability we have ever seen. Let us remember that gratitude is not unserious, that wonder is not childish, and that encouragement is not a lesser form of intelligence.**

The future is not a horror movie. It is not a punishment. It is not a sentence handed down to us by forces we cannot influence. It is something we are building together, imperfectly, unevenly, and in real time. That should make us more responsible, yes, but it should also make us more alive. It should make us more generous with our imagination. I**t should make us more careful about the stories we tell in front of children. It should make us more willing to say, without embarrassment, that this is an incredible time to be here.**

So to the pessimists, with love, I say this: ***cheer the f\*\*\* up.*** Not because everything is easy, and not because everything will work out on its own, but because there is still so much worth building, so much worth protecting, so much worth healing, and so much worth handing forward with hope.

Yours,

Darko
Empathy Is the Strategy: Thriving in the Age of AI

And here’s the business case, because yes, there is one. Products grounded in empathy drive better adoption. Experiences rooted in real human needs create loyalty. AI that understands context reduces friction, returns, and complaints. Empathy, it turns out, is measurable. You’ll find it in your KPIs if you know where to look.

![](/images/articles/empathy-is-the-strategy-thriving-in-the-age-of-ai/3.jpeg)\
June 24, 2025

I’ve sat through enough AI strategy meetings to know the usual arc: someone pulls up a slide with a labyrinth of data pipelines, someone else uses the word “orchestration” three times in a single sentence, and suddenly it feels like we’re launching a spaceship instead of serving people. Don’t get me wrong - models, infrastructure, and systems matter. But they’re not what will determine whether your organization thrives in this new era. The real differentiator? It’s not just your tech. It’s your touch. It’s empathy. That quiet, often-overlooked force that turns good ideas into meaningful change.

Not as a buzzword. Not as a soft skill buried on slide 47 of the org culture deck. Empathy as your operating principle. Your differentiator. Your strategic edge.

The more I work at the intersection of retail, fashion, and AI, the more I realize: ***if your technology doesn’t make people’s lives better, easier, more human, more connected, then what exactly is the point?***

We’re living through a generational shift. AI is reshaping industries, workflows, job descriptions, and even our collective imagination. And in that transformation, there’s a temptation to lead with speed. Ship fast. Implement now. Race to keep up.

But real leadership was never about playing catch-up. It’s not about reacting to the latest trend or rushing to check a box marked “AI-enabled.” Leadership is about having the clarity to see beyond the noise and the courage to decide how you want to show up in that future. It’s about setting the tone, not just meeting the tempo. ***The best leaders don’t just adapt to what’s coming - they shape it, with intention, with vision, and above all, with humanity.***

Empathy isn’t the thing that slows us down. It’s the thing that keeps us from running in the wrong direction.

Too often, I hear AI talked about in extremes. On one side: utopian hype about infinite productivity. On the other hand, dystopian dread that we’re automating ourselves out of existence. The reality, as it usually is, lives in the messy middle. AI has enormous potential - but only if we shape it with care.

John Dewey once said, “A problem well put is half solved.” The way we frame AI’s role in our organizations will define what we build and who it benefits. ***So we have to start with people. The ones using the tools. The ones impacted by the decisions. The ones whose trust we need to earn and keep.***

Design thinking got this right long before AI showed up at the party. Empathize. Define. Ideate. Prototype. Test. Yet somewhere between data ingestion and model optimization, we forgot step one. We forgot to ask what matters to the people we claim to serve.

I’ve seen firsthand how empathy changes the outcome of an AI project. A pilot that works in theory but frustrates store associates in practice? That’s not innovation. That’s disruption without discernment. But when we pause, listen, and adapt, when we respond to the lived experience of our users, we build solutions that stick.

And here’s the business case, because yes, there is one. ***Products grounded in empathy drive better adoption.*** ***Experiences rooted in real human needs create loyalty.*** AI that understands context reduces friction, returns, and complaints. ***Empathy, it turns out, is measurable. You’ll find it in your KPIs if you know where to look.***

Strategically, empathy helps you see around corners. It reveals not just what’s happening, but ***why.*** It surfaces unmet needs, quiet frustrations, and latent potential. And that intelligence? That’s what the best leaders use to make bold, enduring decisions.

***Empathy also builds trust, and trust is the currency of transformation.*** If your teams don’t trust your intent, they’ll resist your roadmap. If your customers don’t trust your experience, they’ll leave your brand. AI will either reinforce that trust or quietly erode it. The choice is ours.

I know it might feel counterintuitive. We’re trained to prioritize logic, efficiency, and output. But as Brené Brown put it, “Clear is kind.***” And being clear about the human impact of our systems is the kindest and most strategic thing we can do.***

This isn’t about being nice. It’s about being real. About telling the truth, especially when it’s uncomfortable. About acknowledging that ***automation without accountability can widen gaps, not close them.*** The decisions we make now will shape work, creativity, and identity for years to come.

Empathy requires courage. It requires slowing down enough to ask better questions. It requires widening the room to include voices that don’t always sit at the tech table. And it requires remembering that ***leadership isn’t just about what we build, it’s about how we build it, and for whom.***

So as we navigate this moment, this inflection point where technology meets humanity, I believe our mandate is clear.

## **Lead with empathy. Embed it into your strategy, your processes, and your metrics. Make it the first step in every project, and the last thing you check before you ship. Treat it not as a moral accessory, but as a core competency.**

Because in the age of AI, the companies that win won’t be the ones that move the fastest. ***They’ll be the ones who remember what it means to be human.***

And they’ll lead the way, not with code, but with care.
I Asked Real Humans About AI Shopping. They Asked Me If I Was Okay.

Our job isn’t to make commerce more futuristic. It’s to make life a little easier. A little calmer. A little more predictable. To reduce the moments where people feel tricked, stuck, or overwhelmed. To build experiences that earn trust the boring way, by working, by being fair, by being easy to undo, and by treating people like humans instead of “conversion opportunities.”

![](/images/articles/i-asked-real-humans-about-ai-shopping-they-asked-me-if-i-was-okay/1771622291301.jpeg)\
**I Love This Future. I Just Don’t Want Us to Forget People.**

I have to start with this: I freaking love technology. I’m a big believer in agentic commerce, and I genuinely can’t wait for it to live up to its full potential. But here’s the thing. I also think we (especially those of us who are true believers) can lose touch with the real world faster than we realize. The real consumer. The real day-to-day shopping chaos. The stuff that doesn’t show up in our decks or demos. So I’m writing this *because* I believe in where this is going, not because I’m skeptical, consider it a friendly little wake-up call to myself (and maybe to anyone else living in the bubble with me).

## **The Experiment**

For the past three months, I’ve been running a little personal experiment: I carved out at least two hours a day, on purpose, to get out of the bubble and talk to people who don’t live and breathe technology. Not in a “user research” way. Just real conversations with friends, family, neighbors, and random people I’d end up chatting with at the store or in line for coffee.

I’d ask simple questions like, “Would you ever let an AI shop for you?” and the reaction was almost always the same: a pause, a half-smile, and then some version of, “Are you okay?”

And honestly…***FAIR!***

Because the more I listened, the more I realized how different our shiny “future of commerce” conversations sound compared to how shopping actually feels to a real person on a random Tuesday.

## **Inside the Bubble vs. Outside the Bubble.**

In our world, we get excited about what’s possible. We talk about AI, identity, personalization, seamless experiences, agent-based journeys, and automation across the lifecycle. We map flows. We imagine a future where your assistant understands you better than you understand yourself and handles the annoying stuff in the background.

***But when you talk to people outside the bubble, you don’t hear “Wow, that sounds efficient.”***

You hear things like: “What if it orders the wrong thing?” “What if I can’t return it?” “What if it chooses something cheap and weird?” “What if it locks me into a subscription?” “What if it starts buying stuff and I don’t notice?” “What if it knows too much about me?” “Who do I talk to when it messes up?”

It’s not that people are anti-technology. A lot of people are just… tired. They’ve been trained by years of pop-ups, fine print, surprise charges, and experiences that feel designed to win against them instead of help them. They’ve learned, sometimes the hard way, that “convenient” often comes with a hidden cost: less control.

## **The Line that Actually Matters**

And that’s when it clicked for me: there’s a big difference between AI helping you shop and AI shopping for you.

Most people I spoke to were open to help. They loved the idea of cutting through noise. They liked the idea of not opening seventeen tabs and comparing the same three products until midnight. They liked the idea of something that remembers preferences and constraints: budget boundaries, delivery needs, brand preferences, “I hate complicated setup,” “I need this by Friday,” “I don’t want to deal with returns.”

***People want relief. They want less mental load.***

But the moment the conversation crossed from “help me decide” into “go ahead and do it,” you could feel the brakes. That line, between assistance and delegation, is where adoption will be won or lost.

And that line is emotional, not technical.

## **Identity Feels Different Out Here**

In tech, we often describe identity as a way to make things smoother: sign in once, faster checkout, better personalization, and more relevance. Outside tech, identity is often experienced as something else entirely: tracking, exposure, risk, losing the ability to explore privately.

A few people said versions of the same thing without even realizing how consistent it was: “I want the convenience, but I don’t want to hand over my whole life.”

They want to browse without feeling watched. They want to explore without feeling profiled. They want to keep their options open without being nudged, pressured, or boxed in.

***They want to share what’s necessary, when it’s necessary, and not a second earlier.***

## **The Part Nobody Puts in Diagrams**

And there’s another piece that doesn’t show up on architecture diagrams: people don’t just want protection from fraud. They want protection from embarrassment.

They don’t want an assistant buying something that makes them feel stupid. They don’t want to explain a weird charge. They don’t want to spend their Saturday untangling a mistake that started with “the system decided.” They don’t want to feel helpless inside a flow they don’t understand.

***So I started thinking about shopping less like a funnel and more like a string of very human moments.***

There’s the moment you realize you need something. The moment you’re trying to figure out what the “right” version is. The moment you’re hovering over the purchase button, wondering if you’re missing something. The moment after you buy, when you just want reassurance that it’s on its way. The moment it arrives, when reality either matches expectations or doesn’t. And then the moment you decide whether you’d ever do that again with the same brand.

When people talk about trust, this is what they mean. Not brand campaigns. Not slogans. Not product launches. They mean: did it arrive on time, did it match what I thought I was buying, and did someone help me when it didn’t?

## **The Future Won’t Land Evenly**

It also made me notice something else: the “future of commerce” isn’t going to land evenly across all categories.

Some purchases are low-risk. Reordering household basics. Buying something you’ve bought before. Replacing a known item in a known size. In those cases, people are far more willing to let automation handle things. It feels like relief.

Other purchases are personal, expensive, or error-intolerant. Things with fit. Taste. Compatibility. Things that become a hassle to return. Things that feel like identity. In those categories, people don’t want speed. They want confidence. They don’t want “one click.” They want “I won’t regret this.”

***You can build the most advanced system in the world, but if it increases the fear of regret, it won’t become a habit.***

## **Capability isn’t Adoption**

And here’s the big lesson I keep coming back to, the one I’m trying to burn into my own brain:

***Just because something exists doesn’t mean it will be adopted.***

Adoption is emotional. Adoption is social. Adoption is cultural. Adoption is when a new behavior becomes easy to digest as normal.

It’s when someone tries it once, and nothing bad happens. It’s when a friend says, “I did it, it worked, it was fine.” It’s when the system feels like it’s on your side. It’s when you feel in control, and you can undo things easily.

## **The Real Question**

So when we talk about AI shaping commerce, I think the real question isn’t “what will agents be capable of?”

**It’s “what will people comfortably delegate without feeling exposed, manipulated, or trapped?”**

The path to that future probably looks less like a sudden leap and more like a gradual handoff. People are happy to let AI reduce overwhelm. Summarize. Compare. Narrow options. Surface trade-offs. Catch mistakes. Remember preferences. Protect them from bad deals.

Then, slowly, they’ll accept AI preparing actions, building carts, drafting purchases, suggesting timing, warning about return policies, and explaining what happens if something goes wrong.

And only after trust is earned, really earned, will they let it act more autonomously. Not because they’re irrational. Because they’re experienced.

## **The Responsibility**

And that’s where I landed after three months of these conversations.

***Not on a hotter take. Not on a new framework. Just on something painfully basic.***

If we’re building the next era of commerce with AI and identity, then we don’t get to build it only for people like us, the ones who have time to learn new flows, who enjoy tinkering, who can tell the difference between a feature and a bug, who know where the settings live. We’re building it for everyone. For the people who are tired after work. For the people juggling kids and errands. For the people who don’t want another account, another password, another “just verify this one more thing,” another system that makes them feel dumb for not understanding it.

***And I think that makes the responsibility pretty clear.***

Our job isn’t to make commerce more futuristic. It’s to make life a little easier. A little calmer. A little more predictable. To reduce the moments where people feel tricked, stuck, or overwhelmed. To build experiences that earn trust the boring way, by working, by being fair, by being easy to undo, and by treating people like humans instead of “conversion opportunities.”

We can get excited about what’s possible, and we should. But we can’t confuse possibility with progress. Progress is when regular people adopt something without thinking about it. When it feels normal. When it quietly helps, instead of loudly demanding attention.

So I’m trying to hold myself to this: go outside the bubble more often, keep having these conversations, and bring that reality back into the room, because “the future” doesn’t belong to the best diagram. It belongs to the people who have to live with what we ship.

***If we keep that straight, if we keep the customer first, keep the basics sacred, and keep the goal simple, we’ll build something worth trusting.***

Not more complex. Just better.
I Got Stuck in Traffic and Realized - From Homepage to Headspace: The Quiet Revolution in How We Shop

I wonder if anyone else obsesses over this stuff the way I do.  Things are moving so fast in tech, in commerce, in how we live and shop and talk to each other, and I’ll be honest, I’m enjoying every minute of the ride. But sometimes, I also catch myself thinking: Are we moving so fast that we’ve stopped noticing how much has already changed?  We’re adapting to new tools, new habits, and new interfaces, almost without realizing it. Change is no longer a moment. It’s a constant. And whether we’re ready or not, it’s happening anyway.  So I wrote something. It started with a traffic jam, a snoring brother-in-law, and an AI that planned my vacation. But it turned into a bigger reflection on where shopping begins now, and what it means when agents, not humans, start the journey.

![](/images/articles/i-got-stuck-in-traffic-and-realized-from-homepage-to-headspace-the-quiet-revolution-in-how-we-shop/1752678039105.png)\
\
Last weekend, I took my family to New York City. It was supposed to be a simple, relaxing getaway. You know, the kind where you leave early, beat traffic, and maybe feel smug about it.

Instead, we spent four hours inching down the highway because, of course, someone thought peak Saturday was the perfect time to repave an entire lane with one lonely guy and a traffic cone army. Bravo.

What should’ve been a two-hour drive turned into an existential podcast, three snack negotiations, and a lot of wondering how we’ve got AI that can write sonnets, but no one’s figured out New York traffic. Honestly… everything evolves. Phones. Shopping. Mars rovers.

But roadwork scheduling in NYC? Untouched since the Bronze Age.

In the backseat, my brother-in-law was snoring with an Olympic-level commitment. My wife was quietly scrolling through old photos and listening to music. And I, stuck in traffic, hands free for once, did something I didn’t plan to do. I opened up ChatGPT and I planned our entire upcoming trip to Macedonia. Then I ordered family gifts… just by asking Alexa. No apps. No tabs. No scrolling. Just words. And it felt easy. Frighteningly easy. By default, stuck in traffic, I thought - “Alright, might as well put my hands to use.” But then it hit me... I didn’t need my hands at all. I could just talk my way through it - and get things done, like magic. That moment stuck with me. Because for the first time, I realized something that had been creeping up for a while:

**More and more, shopping isn’t starting on a homepage. Not always. Not by default.**

It’s starting in a conversation. A quick ask. A moment of intent that happens off-screen. And in the very near future, faster than most of us realize, that conversation won’t even start with me, with us. It’ll start with an AI. Our digital twin. Our super-efficient friend who knows we're traveling soon, remembers Ella’s birthday is next week, and has already filtered for waterproof, under $100, arrive by Tuesday gifts... before we had our first sip of coffee.

That’s not science fiction. That’s just where we’re headed. Sounds wild, I know. But it’s happening.

That’s exciting. And also... kind of terrifying. Because if that’s what a car ride in 2025 feels like, what’s the world going to feel like in 2030? Or 2035? **We’re in a moment of real change.**

Not the slow, buzzwordy kind. The real kind, the kind that sneaks up on you and then one day just… happens. And when you work in tech, retail, product, or anything that touches customers, you start to notice: Times are changing, and even though the screen is still here. It’s not calling all the shots anymore.

For years, we treated the screen like the North Star. We designed around it. We optimized it. We made sure every button, banner, PDP, and scroll felt “just right.” We built for the screen.

Now? **We should start thinking about building through it.** Let me explain.

For the majority of eccomerce existence, people typed in a URL, landed on a homepage, clicked around, and made a decision. It was predictable. Linear. Measurable. Funnel-shaped.

Today, we are at the inception of a new concept that will shape commerce for years to come. It's becoming normalized to hear our loved ones saying things like:

“Hey, can you find me a backpack that’s carry-on size, waterproof, and under $100?” It's for Ella's birthday - need to be here before Wednesday." And before you have the chance to respond, Alexa, or perplexity, or whoever, will say, " Sure, I got you. "

That’s it. **One sentence = one intent = one action.**

The interface is still a screen, well, sometimes. But really, it can be anything now. Any device that’s connected, that listens, that talks back. The main point? Screens aren’t the start of the experience anymore. They’re just one possible stop along the way, or not there at all.

What matters it’s the surface beneath it. The real action? It’s happening in the conversation - whether it’s voice, chat, gesture, or prompt. **We’ve entered the era of agentic interfaces.** Where we don’t just browse. We brief. Where we don’t just click. We command. And when that’s the default, what happens to the beautiful funnel we spent years obsessing over?

**This isn’t a fresh coat of paint, it’s like the whole house got up, moved neighborhoods, and forgot to leave a forwarding address. Because it’s not just the "screen part" of the journey that’s changing. It’s all of it.**

From how we discover products to how we get help after they arrive, every phase of the shopping lifecycle is quietly transforming. Not with fireworks, but with small, meaningful shifts.

**Discovery** used to start with a homepage. Now it might start with a whisper to your new AI Glasses. Or a typed question in your chat app. “I'm sad. What should we do?” - The bot might say - "Let's go Shopping - that always make you smile. Do you want to see the newest collection? " Boom. Five curated options appear, pulled from a dozen storefronts you never visited on your glasses, or phone, or it just describes them for you in detail.

**Evaluation** used to mean comparing tabs, reading reviews, and sorting filters. In our example, it’s a conversation. Your agent knows what you like. What you’ve returned. What your friend just bought. It narrows your choices before you even ask. It filters on your behalf. It suggests based on your mood.

**Ordering** used to be the big finale. Now it’s invisible. A sentence, a nod, a confirmation ping, or completely independent of you, as you told it 4 months ago to find good deals for your 20 year anniversary, and it just happened to have a flash sale. It’s not a journey. It’s a moment. But behind that moment? A hundred micro-decisions your system has to make flawlessly.

**Fulfillment** is under pressure, too. Because a smart assistant doesn’t care about your internal APIs. It cares that the product gets there on time. That it fits. That it works. It will notify you when your inventory is stale. It will remember if the box was beaten up last time.

And **post-purchase?** That might be the most human moment of all. Because the agent helped them shop, but now something has gone wrong. It didn’t arrive. It doesn’t fit. It disappointed. And suddenly, they’re not talking to the agent anymore. **They’re talking to you.**

That’s the moment that matters. That’s the moment they remember. That’s the moment where brands are made - or lost. **So yes, the screen is still here. But it’s no longer the main character.** It’s the quiet helper, the conduit. The journey? It’s happening in real life again. And we have to be ready to meet it. **This also means that your brand’s API becomes your voice. Your product schema becomes your storefront. Your trustworthiness becomes your new conversion rate.**

Take a breath. (I did too.)

Because yeah, this new world? It’s wild. And it’s not just about “letting go of control.” It’s about showing up differently. Here’s the thing. If we want our brands to exist in this next chapter of shopping, we’ve got to start thinking like the agents. **That means being findable, understandable, trustworthy… and honestly, kinda helpful. If the agent doesn’t trust what we’re putting out there, we don’t get surfaced. It’s that simple.**

## **Porter’s Five Forces- A Cheat Sheet**

For those of you who might be saying, "*Hey, I know Porter’s Five Forces, but could use a refresher"* - no worries, I've got your back! This is the framework that helps us understand how industries work and where the power lies. It's like a lightsaber for understanding the business dynamics at play. Here's how each force shapes up when AI enters the scene:



* **Competitive Rivalry:** Is AI making your competitors faster, smarter, or just cooler? Are they passing you on the hyperloop, or are you ahead of the curve?
* **Threat of New Entrants:** Can AI act as a lightsaber-like barrier, protecting your product, or is it like opening a can of Tatooine sandworms, inviting everyone to try their hand?
* **Bargaining Power of Suppliers:** Can AI help you outsmart suppliers like the Rebel Alliance outsmarts the Empire?
* **Bargaining Power of Buyers:** Can AI make your product so irresistible that customers stick with you, or will they be lured away like Han Solo by the promise of a smoother ride?
* **Threat of Substitutes:** Is AI the Force that drives competitors to create alternatives to your product, or is it the same Force that helps you stay ahead of them?

Let’s break it down with a little more detail - and no, I won’t be using any lightsaber sound effects… unless you ask.

Note: I’ll use examples from my world - fulfillment, post-purchase, and order management, but this timeless framework applies to any product space, including yours.

## **How Product Leaders Can Use the Five Forces to Evaluate AI**

**1. Competitive Rivalry: Using AI to Gain an Edge**

In the retail tech world, competitive rivalry is intense and sometimes insane. Let's take, for example, OMS. It will not be far along before an AI-native Order Management System provides a significant advantage. Traditional OMS solutions rely on static rules and manual intervention, but AI-driven systems will offer dynamic, real-time decision-making.

**Example:** Imagine using AI to dynamically reroute orders based on real-time data like inventory levels, carrier capacity, traffic/road conditions, foot traffic in stores, DC capacity, etc. If a fulfillment center faces delays, road conditions worsen, or the store gets busier than usual - the AI-native OMS will autonomously switch to a different location, ensuring customer expectations are met without manual effort.

**Tip:** Regularly benchmark your product’s AI capabilities against competitors in the OMS and returns management space to identify opportunities and threats early. Can you clearly identify a use case that provides a competitive advantage?



**2. Threat of New Entrants: Leveraging AI as a Barrier to Entry**

AI can serve as either a competitive moat or a door opener, depending on how it is leveraged. For product leaders, the key question is whether the AI technology in question can create a unique value proposition that is difficult for new entrants to replicate. Rather than focusing solely on AI as a standalone innovation, its true power often lies in enhancing existing functionalities in ways that fundamentally transform the user experience or operational efficiency. In many cases, AI doesn’t need to reinvent the wheel - it can revolutionize it by making established processes smarter, more efficient, and more personalized.

**Example:** In the near future, AI-driven returns prevention management will proactively detect SLA risks and dynamically optimize order prioritization, secure faster carriers in real-time, and tailor product exchanges based on customer preferences and past purchases. This advanced predictive intelligence will not only enhance operational efficiency but also create a formidable competitive advantage. Given that these AI models rely on personalized data to uphold individualized SLAs, new entrants will face significant challenges in replicating this level of precision and adaptability.

**Tip: I**dentify where AI could provide unique insights or efficiencies in post-purchase and returns management that would be challenging for new competitors to replicate.



**3. Bargaining Power of Suppliers: Strengthening Supplier Relationships with AI**

AI can play a pivotal role in reshaping supplier dynamics by improving demand forecasting, optimizing procurement strategies, and enhancing negotiation capabilities. By leveraging AI-driven insights, product leaders can proactively manage supplier relationships, reducing dependency risks and ensuring more favorable terms.

**Example:** A retailer leveraging an AI-powered inventory management system can accurately forecast inventory needs, reducing both overstock and stockouts. AI can also analyze real-time market trends, competitor pricing, and supplier performance data to uncover cost-saving opportunities. For B2B operations, an AI-driven system can intelligently recommend the optimal timing for bulk orders based on price fluctuations. Additionally, it can proactively identify supplier risks and even autonomously onboard and contract alternative suppliers - ensuring a more agile and resilient supply chain.

**Tip:** Be open-minded about combining AI-driven supplier analytics with emerging technologies like blockchain and smart contracts. Conduct ongoing research to monitor AI’s crossover with blockchain in automating supplier agreements, ensuring transparency, and reducing fraud. Leveraging AI for forecasting and blockchain for secure, self-executing contracts can enhance negotiation strategies and create a more resilient supply chain.



**4. Bargaining Power of Buyers: Enhancing Customer Experience with AI**

Hyper-personalization is set to become the new normal. In the near future, we won’t even call it “personalization” anymore - it will simply be the expected way of doing business. AI will empower product leaders to shape this new reality, delivering deeply tailored experiences that, in turn, reduce churn and strengthen customer loyalty.

But what does this mean for the *bargaining power of buyers?*

In short - brands will understand customers better than ever, reshaping the balance of power in commerce. This will increase brand stickiness and reduce price sensitivity. This means, that we MUST also drive demand for ethical AI, data transparency, and AI-powered consumer negotiation tools.

**Example:** From above - hyper-personalize shopping experiences. The system predicts not only a customer’s style preferences but also suggests outfits based on upcoming weather, recent purchases, and even their social calendar. Over time, the AI fine-tunes recommendations, making it - a personal stylist. Combining this with AI-driven personal pricing, the customer becomes deeply engaged with the brand, making it harder to switch to a competitor. In customer care, AI can analyze past interactions and predict the best support channels or even preemptively solve issues before customers reach out.

**Tip:** Explore the evolution of loyalty programs beyond discounts. AI-driven personalization can transform them into personal stylists or tailored shopping assistants. By integrating hyper-personalized recommendations, predictive styling, and exclusive early access based on individual preferences, brands can create deeper emotional connections. This shift makes loyalty a core part of the experience, not just a perk, increasing retention and making switching brands feel like losing a friend.

**5. Threat of Substitutes: The AI Arms Race & Competitive Differentiation**

AI is a double-edged sword. It lowers the barrier to entry for competitors while offering early adopters a chance to build a defensible advantage. The longer you wait, the more difficult it becomes to differentiate, as AI-driven capabilities quickly become industry standards. You don’t want to rush implementation, but doing nothing means risking obsolescence.

**Example:** Returns have long been considered a necessary evil - an unavoidable cost of doing business. Customers send items back, wait for approval, and eventually get a refund or exchange. It’s a **static, transactional process**, and frankly, a missed opportunity.

But what if **returns could be a strategic differentiator?**

We are at the **inception** of this transformation. Some retailers have already started tailoring return experiences based on **loyalty tiers and purchase history**, offering faster refunds or personalized exchanges to high-value customers. But this is just the beginning. As product leaders, now is the time to **think beyond the obvious** and explore how AI can reshape the returns experience in ways that don’t even exist yet.

Imagine this:



* **Try Before You Return:** Instead of shipping an item back immediately, AI-powered **augmented reality (AR) or digital styling tools** could help customers test out alternative options first. Found the perfect replacement? AI processes the exchange before the return even happens.
* **Returns Meet the Resale Market:** What if AI could **match your return to another buyer** before it even leaves your hands? The system scans demand in real-time and suggests selling directly to another customer at a discount—turning returns into a frictionless resale opportunity.
* **Refunds, But Smarter:** Returns don’t have to mean a full refund. AI could assess **real-time demand and item desirability** to offer **partial refunds, trade-in credits, or even higher-value incentives** for keeping the item.
* **Subscription Models Get Smarter:** For fashion rentals, electronics, and beauty brands, AI could **predict return likelihood** based on **wear-and-tear, sentiment analysis, or usage tracking**—preemptively swapping out items before they become a problem.
* **Sustainable Returns by Default:** Instead of reflexively sending every return back to a warehouse, AI could **determine the most eco-friendly processing route** based on item condition, location, and environmental impact. Want to reduce your carbon footprint? Customers choosing **in-store drop-offs or lower-impact return methods** could earn **loyalty points or discounts** as an incentive.



**Tip:** Regularly evaluate emerging AI technologies that could disrupt the post-purchase and returns management space. AI isn’t just making returns easier - it’s redefining them. The brands that move first will set new consumer expectations, turning returns into a loyalty driver instead of a loss. The question isn’t if this shift will happen—it’s who will own it first.

## **Building AI into Your Product Strategy**

As I mentioned before, all of the examples above come from my area of expertise. However, I truly believe that this framework is universally applicable. The key is to master the fundamentals. Here’s my recommendation:



* Use Porter’s Five Forces as a framework to evaluate AI use cases - think of it as your map to the galaxy’s potential.
* Prioritize AI initiatives that align with your long-term product vision. Don’t just chase every shiny object (unless it’s the Millennium Falcon).
* Stay agile. AI is evolving fast - so should your roadmap. If you don’t evolve, you’ll end up like the Death Star - destroyed by a small but clever attack.
* Test, learn, and iterate - AI thrives on data. Keep feeding it and refining your approach, just like the Jedi constantly honing their skills.
* Involve cross-functional teams early to uncover AI opportunities and avoid pitfalls. Think of it as gathering your Rebel Alliance before embarking on an epic mission.

### **Final Thoughts**

AI isn’t just a buzzword. it’s a strategic game-changer. Or is it?

By using Michael Porter’s Five Forces, you can take a structured, no-nonsense approach to understanding how AI could transform your product strategy - without the chaos of chasing trends.

But here’s the catch. Jumping into AI without a framework is like strapping a hyperdrive onto a broken ship. You’ll burn through fuel, but you won’t get anywhere. Many enterprise retailers fall into this trap, rushing into AI out of FOMO, only to struggle with real business impact.

Instead, think of AI as your trusted co-pilot, helping you:



Outmaneuver competitors

1. Fortify against new entrants
2. Strengthen supplier partnerships
3. Deepen customer loyalty
4. Stay ahead of substitutes



Or, in the wise words of Master Yoda: “**Use AI wisely, you must**.” Stay curious, humble, and always in Padawan mode - learning, experimenting, and adapting.

### **AI Isn’t Magic - It’s Math (With a Messy Middle)**

There’s a tendency to treat AI like a magic wand - wave it, and out comes perfectly tagged data, personalized content, and automated everything. But let’s be real. It’s more like a math problem written in disappearing ink… over a moving target.

AI learns from your data - and all the glorious, messy, edge-case-laden context that comes with it. That means:

* It **reflects** your inconsistencies.
* It **inherits** your assumptions.
* And it **exposes** where your systems aren't quite as tidy as you'd hoped.

For years, digital commerce trained customers to navigate. Type in the search bar. Choose from a menu. Filter by size. Sort by price. Open six tabs. Compare three products. Forget why you started. Get distracted. Buy socks instead. It worked, mostly, because it was the best model available at the time. But it was always asking the customer to do a lot of translation work.

***Now that translation work is starting to move into the system.***

This is where I think so many people are underestimating what is actually happening. What we call **agentic commerce** sounds futuristic, slightly intimidating, and honestly a little too polished as a phrase. But when you strip away the jargon, it is simply the next stage of this shift. It is commerce that helps. Commerce that interprets. Commerce that carries intent. Commerce that can increasingly take action alongside the customer, and sometimes on the customer’s behalf. **That means shopping will feel less like navigating a store and more like continuing a conversation.**

A customer will not just search for “black dress.” She will say, “I need something for a fall wedding, not too formal, can be worn again, preferably flattering but easy.” Or, “I need jeans for a trip, good on planes, polished enough for dinner, not stiff.” Or, “I want a gift for my brother that says I tried, but not too hard.” That is not a search behavior problem. That is a human behavior reality. **And the commerce systems that win will be the ones that understand what people mean, not just what they type.**

This is already beginning. Discovery is moving into chat interfaces, publisher ecosystems, recommendation layers, social platforms, digital assistants, and new surfaces that do not always look like commerce until a purchase suddenly happens there. **The storefront is no longer the only place the shopping journey lives.** In some cases, it is not even where the journey starts. As someone who works in commerce, I do not see this as a novelty. I see it as a structural shift.

And yes, I also see the panic. Every time a new tool shows up, half the internet acts like we will all be replaced by lunchtime. Then, twenty minutes later, those same people are using it to summarize a document, write a brief, plan a trip, or organize a meeting no one wanted in the first place. **We are in this strange phase where we are both terrified and deeply attached to our own productivity gains.** I understand that tension because I live it too.

I used to make books for my niece that would take me months. Real months. Writing, revising, formatting, designing, obsessing, reworking, and generally behaving like the world’s most underpaid boutique publishing house. Now I can do something equally thoughtful in two hours. Not because I care less. Because the tools have changed. And if I am being honest, I would be ridiculous to pretend I have not changed with them. We all have.

That does not mean all change is good. It does mean pretending nothing is changing is not a strategy. For commerce leaders, the job now is not to romanticize the old funnel. It is to understand what the customer is becoming accustomed to, and then build responsibly for that future. That is why I keep coming back to loyalty. Because the real risk in this next era is not simply that technology changes the buying journey. Technology always changes the buying journey.

### **The real risk is that the relationship between brand and customer gets abstracted one layer further away, and brands wake up too late to realize that the interface now owns the intimacy.**

That should concern all of us. If customers begin discovering, evaluating, and transacting across assistant-led or agent-mediated environments, then loyalty cannot stay trapped inside one owned channel. It cannot be something that only functions if the customer comes back through the exact same front door every time. In a world of context compression, **loyalty has to become portable**. **By that I mean this: wherever the customer is, our ability to care for them has to travel with them**.

If they discover us through an AI assistant, we should still be able to serve them well. If they start their journey through a publisher, we should still be able to recognize value in that relationship. If they are loyal to us, that loyalty should still matter when the interface changes. The customer should not lose the benefits of trust, recognition, relevance, and service just because commerce has become more distributed.

That is a design problem. A systems problem. A strategy problem. And most of all, **a leadership problem**. **It is our responsibility to adapt. It is our responsibility to build for this world before someone else builds it for us.**

**It is our responsibility to ensure that as the path to purchase becomes more compressed, more conversational, and more agentic, the customer experience becomes more human, not less.**

That means building systems that preserve trust. Building experiences that understand intent. Building commerce that works across channels without losing brand integrity. Building loyalty models that are resilient enough to travel. Building governance that keeps innovation from becoming chaos. Building with enough humility to admit that the customer is changing faster than our org charts are.

Because that, ultimately, is where this is going.

We are moving toward a world in which context follows the customer more fluidly than ever before. Shopping will be embedded in more places. Discovery will happen in more surfaces. Recommendations will become more dynamic. Interfaces will become more conversational. Assistance will become more intelligent. And the brands that win will not simply be the brands with the best products or the loudest media spend. They will be the brands that understand the behavioral shift underneath all of it.

### **That shift is context compression. It is the collapse of distance between intention and action.**

And once you see it, you start to realize it is not just changing commerce. It is changing people. Which means, whether we feel ready or not, it is changing the job of everyone building the future of commerce too.
The Most Important Thing 2025 Reminded Me About Technology
Article about the most important thing 2025 reminded me about technology.

![](/images/articles/the-most-important-thing-2026-reminded-me-about-technology/1767022140511.png)

I was raised by parents who didn’t really like technology. My father, especially, was convinced it would eventually hinder humanity. Not in a polite “let’s be thoughtful” way. More in a “this is how society ends” way.

When I was younger, I argued with him like it was a competitive sport. Progress is progress, the future is inevitable, and humanity always adapts. You know the vibe. Confident. Certain. Slightly insufferable.

In 2026, I finally understood what he was really trying to protect.

Because this year has been… a lot. In the best way and in the “wait, that happened already?” way. It is genuinely such a privilege to live and work in this time. Everything is moving so fast that sometimes I feel like my brain needs a software update before my next meeting. If you love technology, if you love building, if you love that moment when you realize the world just quietly changed again, it’s hard not to feel grateful. We get to experience the future arriving in real time.

And yet, I can hear my father’s voice in the background, not saying “I told you so,” but asking something softer: “Okay. But what happens to people while all this is happening?”

That question has become my anchor. And honestly, it’s the question that’s shaped the way I think about product leadership more than any trend report or keynote ever could.

I’ve also been lucky, and I don’t say that lightly, to be part of an organization where leadership is aligned on a simple idea: put the human, the employee, and the customer first. In practice, that changes everything. It changes what you prioritize. It changes what you measure. It changes how you talk about trade-offs. It’s one thing to say “people first” in a deck. It’s another thing to feel it show up when timelines are tight, when the market is loud, and when everyone is tempted to chase whatever is shiny that week.

This year reminded me that as product leaders, it’s not only our job to ship. It’s our job to choose. And our choices shape how technology shows up in people’s lives. So everything I’m about to say is less “here is the truth” and more “here is what I’ve noticed from the inside, with equal parts awe and caution.”

I’ve been thinking about 2026 through the customer journey lens, because it forces me to stay honest. Customers don’t experience our roadmaps. They experience their own lives, and they invite our products into them.

## **Discovery is where I felt the ground move the most.**

For years, we treated search like the front door. In 2026, I’m not sure it’s even a door anymore. It’s more like a conversation happening everywhere at once, with people asking AI the kinds of questions they used to type into a search bar. And if you spend any time watching Gen Z, it becomes obvious that “Googling” isn’t always the default behavior. They ask. They chat. They get a summary, an opinion, a shortlist, and sometimes a therapist-adjacent response in the same exchange.

And then there’s the relationship layer, which is the part that still makes me pause. People are not just using AI as a tool. They’re bonding with it. The exact numbers can vary depending on what you read, but the direction is undeniable. The emotional connection is real. That means discovery is no longer only about “how do we show up.” It’s also about “how do we earn trust in a more intimate interface.”

That intimacy is exciting, but it is also weighty. Because when discovery becomes conversational, it becomes personal. People ask questions they wouldn’t ask a website. They share context they wouldn’t share in a form field. That changes the bar for responsibility.

What makes all of this feel even more surreal is how quickly the underlying technology moves. Models can feel almost AGI-ish to everyday users because the experience is so fluent. And features that used to differentiate products for years now get copied in weeks. Sometimes I’ll see a “big announcement,” feel impressed, go to sleep, and wake up to three alternatives and an open-source clone built by someone who apparently doesn’t need rest.

On the work side, a few tools genuinely changed the way teams operate. Not “nice to have” changes. Real changes. The kind that compresses the distance between an idea and a prototype, or between a messy thought and a clear narrative. If you’ve used tools like Claude Code, Wispr, Nano Banana Pro, or NotebookLM, you know what I mean. It’s not just speed. It’s that subtle shift in what you consider possible in a day.

But here’s where I try to stay humble: just because something is impressive doesn’t mean it’s stable. AI labs are growing revenue, but a lot of the economics still look like “spend now, reap later.” That creates volatility. It shapes pricing, partnerships, and the lifecycle of products we might bet on. It also reinforces a lesson I’ve had to repeat to myself all year: acceleration is not the same as certainty.

Now, one of the reasons I feel all of this so personally is that I’ve watched my parents’ relationship with technology evolve in a way that still makes me smile and ache at the same time.

When I was very young, my parents and I took a trip to Athens, Greece. We stayed at a hotel, and in the bathroom, there was something we had never seen before: a faucet with a sensor. You put your hands underneath, and the water magically comes out.

To me, it was the future.

To my parents, it was an emergency.

I still remember my dad marching down to the front desk, deeply concerned, to announce that the faucet was broken. Not “maybe it’s broken.” Broken. Defective. Dangerous, probably. And my mom was right there with him, validating the situation like, “Yes, yes, we tried everything. No water. Very serious.”

Somewhere in that hotel, a poor employee had to explain that the faucet was not broken. It was just… smarter than we were.

And the funniest part is that this wasn’t ancient history. This was maybe twenty-something years ago. It’s not like we were in the 1800s discovering electricity. It was a faucet. A faucet that could sense hands. And it completely short-circuited our understanding of reality.

I think about that story a lot now, because in a weird way, 2026 sometimes feels like we’re all standing at the front desk again, trying to explain that something is broken, when actually the world just changed underneath us.

But here’s the part that makes it more than a funny travel story.

Today, my parents are both very sick. Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. The kinds of diseases that don’t just affect memory and movement. They reshape identity. They shift the atmosphere in a home. They introduce a loneliness that isn’t always visible from the outside.

And technology, the thing my father feared, is also one of the things that makes life a little easier now.

One of the most meaningful things I’ve done this year is build a custom GPT for my father in our native language. He can talk to it and ask questions about both diseases in the way he naturally thinks and speaks. And my dad, who once escalated a sensor faucet like it was a hotel crisis, now has an AI that he can ask, “What should I expect next?” or “Why is this happening?” or “What does this symptom mean?”

Does it cure anything? No.

But it helps his mental state. It gives him a sense of agency. It gives him something steady to talk to on days when the world feels confusing and small. It meets him where he is, without judgment, without fatigue, without making him feel like a burden for asking the same question twice.

And there’s another layer that still gets me. I’m the one who built it. Me. The kid who went to law school and then transitioned into technology. That fact alone would have sounded ridiculous to my younger self. It’s also a reminder of how accessible this technology has become for our generation. The tools are powerful, but they’re also closer to everyday life than ever before. In some ways, my parents’ generation missed out on that bridge. They missed out on the years where technology could have been a companion, not a threat.

So when I talk about being grateful to work in this time, I’m not only talking about the pace of innovation. I’m talking about moments like that, where a human need meets a new kind of capability, and for a second, the future feels less like disruption and more like care.

## **This brings me to what I think is the most strategically interesting shift happening right now: Agentic Commerce.**

We are watching the industry collectively lean forward. Major players are pushing toward agent-enabled payments and commerce experiences. Everyone is experimenting. Everyone is moving. And it’s easy to feel like we are already behind.

But I honestly think we’re still at the beginning.

The real question isn’t technical. It’s marketplace-level.

What happens when every surface becomes a marketplace opportunity?

If intent can show up anywhere, and discovery becomes conversational, and the “storefront” can be an interface you don’t control, then we need to rethink what it means to be present. We might be moving into a world where “being findable” is not a channel strategy. It is the strategy.

And yes, there’s a provocative question inside that: will websites matter in five to ten years? I don’t think it’s a clean yes or no. Websites won’t disappear overnight. But the center of gravity may shift upstream, into the conversation, into the moment a customer says, “I need something for Friday night, I don’t want to think too hard, and please don’t make me return it.”

In that world, we need to position ourselves to meet the customer wherever intent is strongest. That means optimizing every surface, including our own. And it means being humble about timing. Agentic checkout will come, but adoption curves are not something we can manifest with optimism. Consumers adopt when it is genuinely better, not just new. Ecosystems mature when identity, fraud, returns, and accountability are solved, not when a demo looks magical.

So the posture I’m trying to hold is this: stay ready, stay visible, and don’t confuse speed with certainty.

Then there’s post-purchase, which I used to think of as the “after” part of the journey. In 2026, I’ve stopped thinking of it that way.

The lines are blurring so much that waterfall phases feel like an internal artifact more than a customer reality. The agent that helps you ask “where is my order?” is increasingly the same kind of intelligence that can help you choose the right item in the first place. The same system can recommend, explain, reassure, troubleshoot, and learn your preferences over time.

So post-purchase becomes table stakes, yes. But it also becomes brand-defining. Because when something goes wrong, customers don’t remember your org chart. They remember whether you showed up. Whether it was easy. Whether it felt respectful. Whether they felt like a person.

One more thing I can’t shake: we still haven’t seen the AI device revolution yet.

We are using this technology on devices that were not designed for it. We’re basically running a new operating system on old hardware and pretending that’s the end state. When the device layer shifts, interaction patterns will shift again. We don’t need to predict the exact form factor to plan for that. We just need to build strategies that are resilient to interface change.

And now, the part I care about most.

**The human part.**

I believe the AI that remembers you is fundamentally better than the AI that does not. From a customer perspective, that’s obvious. Remembering preferences, context, fit, style, what mattered last time. That’s how you reduce friction in a way that feels like care.

But “remembering” sits on a thin line. Helpful on one side. Creepy on the other.

T**he difference is trust, transparency, and control.**

Data security and privacy are still developing in this space. That means we don’t get to treat them as checkboxes. They need to be foundational. Baked in. Designed deliberately. And as product leaders, we don’t get to outsource that responsibility. We can and should partner with Legal and Security and data teams, but we set the tone in what we ask for, what we allow, and what we refuse to build.

If 2025 taught me anything, it’s that being people-first is not a slogan. It’s a daily set of decisions. Choosing clarity over hype. Choosing guardrails over shortcuts. Choosing long-term trust over short-term lift.

I’m optimistic. Truly. This era could become one of the most meaningful leaps in how we learn, work, create, and care for each other.

And I’m cautious too. Because uncharted territory always comes with hidden risks, and the costs are rarely distributed evenly.

Maybe my father wasn’t warning me about technology after all. Maybe he was warning me about forgetting who technology is for.

I’m trying not to forget.
We Optimize for Every Metric Except the One That Actually Matters

We built AI that can predict your next purchase before you've thought of it. We have never had more power to actually understand people. Not just their data - them. The generation before us built the internet. They gave us speed, scale, and reach. What we build now, the values we wire into these systems today, is what the next generation will inherit as normal. We don't get a second chance to decide what AI cares about. That decision is being made right now, in roadmaps and backlogs and sprint cycles, by people like us. Let's make sure we leave them something worth inheriting.

![](/images/articles/we-optimize-for-every-metric-except-the-one-that-actually-matters/1.jpeg)

July 1, 2026

A few weeks ago I started getting ads for baby diapers.

Then onesies. Then a stroller comparison guide, and a newsletter about sleep training. The internet had made up its mind: **there was a baby in my house.**

There isn't. I was buying diapers for my parents.

My father has Parkinson's. My mother has Alzheimer's. Somewhere in my browsing, a system noticed the word "diapers," reached for the most statistically likely story, and decided I was a new dad. It was fast. It was efficient. It was, in its own way, impressive. And it understood nothing at all about the person it was selling to.

I've thought about that machine a lot since, because thinking about machines like that - it is my job.

I lead AI Strategy for consumers. Stripped of the title, my work is to figure out how artificial intelligence should show up for our customers, where it belongs in their journey, what it should do, and what it should never do, so that it makes their lives genuinely easier instead of just louder. I don't build the systems. I help decide where we point them. And the diaper machine is the perfect picture of the thing I worry we're getting wrong. It did exactly what it was designed to do. The failure wasn't the technology. The failure was what we decided was worth measuring.

We are very, very good at convenience. We can shave seconds off a checkout, predict your next purchase, reorder your groceries before you've noticed you're out. All of it is countable, so all of it gets optimized. Care is different. Care is noticing that a man buying adult diapers might be holding his family together, not starting one. Care is not making him explain that. Care resisted measurement, so somewhere along the way we quietly stopped trying to deliver it, and told ourselves that convenience was the same thing, because on the dashboard the numbers looked identical.

They are not the same thing. Convenience gets the package to your door by Friday. Care understands that the package was never the point.

I want to be careful here, because this is the part people get wrong. I am not someone who fears the machine. I am the opposite. I am alive to how much these tools have given the people I love.

My father, as a young man, wrote letters to his own dying mother hundred of miles away, and waited weeks for a reply that sometimes came after she was gone. I talk to my parents three times a day. My niece was born early, spent two and a half years in a hospital, and was described to us in terms of all the things she would never do. She does most of them now. **Technology is part of the reason I get to hug her.**

So when I say convenience is not care, I am not romanticizing some warmer, slower past. The past was letters into silence. I'll take the video call. What I'm saying is harder than nostalgia: we now hold the most context-aware tools in human history, and the question is no longer whether they can understand people. It's whether we'll ask them to.

**And that is the strategic question of this moment, not a philosophical one.**

We are past the proof-of-concept. AI is being embedded into customer experiences right now, at scale, by teams with roadmaps and deadlines and conversion targets. The systems being built this year will shape what a relationship between a brand and a person looks like for the next decade. The design decisions being made in backlogs today, what signals to read, what context to carry, what to infer and what to ask, those are not engineering decisions. They are values decisions. They just happen to be wearing the clothing of engineering decisions.

Personalization is often framed as the answer. I'd argue it's only the answer if we define it correctly. Personalization isn't knowing my size and my purchase history. It's knowing that the same word, "diapers", can mean two completely opposite chapters of a life, and that which chapter you assume tells your customer everything about whether you're actually paying attention.

The machine that invented a baby could just as easily have paused and grasped a quieter, truer story, a son, far from home, trying to care for the two people who once cared for him. It had everything it needed to understand. We just never told it that understanding was the goal. We told it that speed was.

**To the leaders deciding how AI enters their customers' lives: this is the window.** Not next year, when the systems are entrenched and the incentives are locked. Now, while the architecture is still being written. The question isn't whether to deploy AI in your customer experience. That decision is already made. The question is what you instruct it to optimize for, and whether you have the courage to put something on that list that doesn't show up cleanly in a dashboard.

I know which one I'd want, on the days I'm buying diapers for my parents.

I know which one would have known they weren't for a baby.

At first it sounds discouraging. Billions invested, so many brilliant people working tirelessly, and yet most projects don’t make it to the finish line. But here’s the perspective I hold on to: those 95% aren’t failures, they are progress in motion.
